subtitle.text: My name is Huckleberry Finn. If you've read a book called The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, you already know about me.
But if you haven't, it doesn't matter.
At the end of that book, my friend Tom and I found six thousand dollars, and each of us was allowed to keep half.
Judge Thatcher invested the money for us, so Tom and I would never have to worry about not having enough money again.
I didn't have a home, so the Widow Douglas took me in.
She said she was going to civilize me.
She made me wear new clean clothes, and sit at the table to eat my meals.
But I missed the way I used to live, wearing my old rags and fixing my own supper.
The widow had a sister, Miss Watson, who was determined to teach me to spell. I couldn't help wiggling around.
"Huckleberry, sit up straight!" she scolded me. "Why can't you try to behave?"
All I could think about was how I wanted to get away.
I needed a change, but I knew the widow and her sister would never understand, so I didn't try to explain.
By the time I went up to my room for bed, I felt sad and lonesome.
I sat in a chair by the window and looked out at the night.
I heard an owl hooting and a dog howling.
It sounded to me as if they were mourning for someone who had died.
It scared me, and I started to tremble.
Then a spider crawled up on my shoulder, and when I shook it off, it fell into my candle and burned up.
I knew that killing a spider could bring me very bad luck, so to keep the bad luck away, I turned myself around three times while crossing my chest.
But I still felt afraid, and I trembled even harder.
I sat there a long time until I calmed down.
Finally, I heard the clock in the town of St. Petersburg strike 12 times.
It was midnight. A twig snapped out in the darkness, and then I heard a little "Me-yow, me-yow," down in the yard.
"Me-yow," I called back softly. Then I climbed out the window, onto the shed, and down to the ground.
And sure enough, there was Tom waiting for me.
Tom and I tiptoed through the widow's garden.
As we passed the kitchen, I tripped over a root.
Jim, Miss Watson's black slave, was sitting by the kitchen door when he heard the noise.
"Who's that?" he called out.
Then he came out into the garden and stood right between us.
Tom and I stood completely still. Jim couldn't see us in the dark.
"I know I heard something," Jim said. "I'm going to sit down here and listen until I hear that sound again."
Well, first my ankle and my ear started to itch, and then my nose.
I felt as if I'd die if I couldn't scratch, but if I did, Jim would know we were there.
Just when I couldn't stand it any more, we heard Jim snoring. He had fallen asleep!
Before we left, Tom played a trick on Jim.
He crept over to Jim, took off his hat, and hung it on a branch.
Tom said that Jim would think witches had moved his hat.
Tom and I went into town where Ben Rogers, Joe Harper, and two or three other boys were waiting for us.
We rowed a boat about four kilometers down the Mississippi River, and came ashore.
There Tom led us to his secret cave, which had an entrance hidden by bushes.
We lit our candles and crawled through a long passageway on our hands and knees.
When we reached the cave, it was damp and cold.
"We'll start a band of robbers called Tom Sawyer's Gang," Tom said.
"Everyone who wants to join must take an oath and write his name in blood."
Everyone agreed. Tom got out a piece of paper and wrote down the oath.
It said that we had to promise to be loyal to the band and never tell its secrets. Anyone who told would be killed.
We all said it was a very good oath, and Tom said that he got the words for it from books about pirates and robbers.
Then Ben said that he thought the families of the boys who told secrets should be killed too. So Tom added that to the oath.
Joe pointed out that I didn't have a family.
Tom replied that I had a father, but the others objected that he'd disappeared a long time ago.
Finally, I said I was willing to give them Miss Watson to kill.
Everyone agreed to that. Then we all stuck our fingers with a pin, and made a mark on the paper with our blood.
"Now," said Ben, "What is our gang going to do?"
"We're going to wear masks and stop carriages on the road," Tom explained.
"We'll kill the people and take their watches and money."
It was getting very late, so we decided to meet again next week to decide which folks we would rob and kill. Then we all went home.
By the time I climbed in my window at the widow's house it was almost dawn.
My new clothes were covered with dirt and I was very tired.
The next day, the Widow Douglas washed the mud off my clothes.
She didn't scold me, but she looked so sad that I decided to try to be good for a while.
I called my father "Pap." No one had seen him for over a year.
That was fine with me. I didn't want to see Pap again because he beat me.
Then some people in St. Petersburg told me that they'd found his body in the river.
They said the drowned man was just his size, with ragged clothes and long hair like Pap's.
But they really couldn't recognize the face because the body had been in the water for so long.
They buried the drowned man on the riverbank.
A few days later, though, I thought of something.
The townspeople told me they found the body floating on his back.
But I had once been told that drowned men floated on their faces and only drowned women floated on their backs.
So I decided the body must have been a woman, dressed up in men's clothes.
After that, I was worried that my father would come back someday.
I still played robbers sometimes with Tom and the other boys, but I was getting bored with it. It was all pretending.
On Saturday Tom told us that we were going to ambush some rich merchants who had two hundred elephants,
six hundred camels, and a thousand mules loaded with diamonds.
But that was just a story he made up.
Really we were just ambushing a Sunday school picnic.
We chased the children away, but only got their doughnuts and jam.
"I don't see any diamonds," I said to Tom.
"Why, they're all right in front of you," Tom answered.
"And the elephants and camels too. Some magicians must have turned them into a Sunday school picnic before we got here."
Then Tom told me how magicians use genies to help them.
"Let's get some genies to come and help us," I said.
Tom explained that you have to rub a magic lamp to make a genie appear.
Then the genie will do whatever you want.
A few days later I thought I would try it.
I went out into the woods with an old lamp and I rubbed it and rubbed it, but nothing happened.
I think Tom really believed these things, but I didn't.
Several months passed, and winter came. I went to school.
At first I hated it, but soon I could spell and read and write a little.
I could say the multiplication tables up to six times seven. Then, school became easier for me.
I was also getting used to the Widow Douglas' house.
The widow told me that I was doing well. She said she wasn't ashamed of me.
One morning at breakfast, I accidentally knocked over the salt shaker.
It is very bad luck to spill salt.
So I reached for some of the salt to throw over my left shoulder because that's supposed to keep the bad luck away.
But Miss Watson stopped me. "Take your hands away, Huckleberry," she scolded. "What a mess you are always making!"
As I left the house after breakfast, I wondered when my bad luck would arrive.
Then I saw footprints in the new snow.
When I bent down to take a closer look, I noticed a cross made with big nails on the heel of the left boot. I knew that boot!
I ran as fast as I could to Judge Thatcher's house.
"Why, my boy, you're all out of breath," he said. "Did you come to get some of your money?"
"No sir," I said. "I don't want it! I want to give all the money to you."
Judge Thatcher was very surprised. He asked me whether anything was wrong.
"Please take it," I begged him, "and don't ask me anything—then I won't have to tell you any lies."
Finally the judge agreed to buy my money from me for one dollar.
He put the dollar in my hand and I left his house.
Miss Watson's black slave Jim, had a magic hairball as big as your fist.
It had come from the fourth stomach of an ox.
Jim said there was a spirit inside it that could see the future.
I went to see Jim that evening. I told him that I knew Pap was back and I wanted to know what he would do.
Jim got out his hairball and said some strange words to it that I couldn't understand.
Then he held it out and dropped it on the floor.
He got down on his knees, put his ear against the hairball, and listened closely. He shook his head.
"The hairball won't talk without money," Jim said.
I gave Jim an old brass quarter that I had in my pocket.
It wasn't a real coin, but maybe the hairball would take it.
Jim put the quarter under the hairball and listened again.
This time, Jim said the hairball would tell me my whole fortune.
The hairball talked to Jim, and Jim repeated it to me:
"Your father doesn't know yet what he's going to do, but you're going to be all right.
You'll have a lot of trouble in your life, but also joy.
And keep away from water as much as you can."
But when I lit my candle and went up to my room that night, there was Pap!
The window was open, so I knew Pap had climbed in using the shed.
For a while we just looked at each other.
I used to be scared of Pap all the time because he beat me so much.
I was scared now, for a minute, but then I looked at him more closely.
Pap was about fifty years old now, and he looked his age.
His skin was as white as a fish belly, and he had long tangled greasy black hair.
His clothes were just rags, and his toes stuck out through the ends of his boots.
Finally Pap said, "Those are starchy clothes you're wearing.
You're educated too, they say—you can read and write.
You think you're better than your father now, don't you, because I can't read?
Who told you that you could do this foolishness, huh?"
"The Widow Douglas. She told me," I said.
"The widow, huh? Well, I'll teach her not to interfere.
And listen to me. You drop that school or I'll give you a beating.
I won't let people bring up a boy to think he's better than his own father! Say, let me hear you read."
I picked up a book and began to read aloud.
After half a minute, he knocked the book out of my hand.
"It's true," he said. "You can do it."
Then he went on, "I see you have a bed, a mirror, and a carpet on the floor—while your own father has to sleep with the pigs.
I've been in town for two days, and I keep hearing that you're rich. That's why I came."
"I don't have any money," I said.
"That's a lie. Judge Thatcher is keeping it for you.
You get me that money tomorrow. I want it!"
Then Pap made me give him the dollar I had in my pocket.
He said he was going to town to get some whiskey.
The next day Pap was drunk. He went to Judge Thatcher's and threatened him, but Judge Thatcher wouldn't give him the money.
Judge Thatcher and the Widow Douglas wanted to take me away from Pap and have one of them be my guardian.
There was a new judge in court, however, who had just come to town.
He didn't know what my father was like.
The judge said that the courts shouldn't split up families.
He said that I had to stay with Pap.
As soon as my father heard this, he told me that he'd beat me until I was covered with bruises unless I got him some money.
I borrowed three dollars from Judge Thatcher and gave it to Pap, and he used the money to get drunk.
Later at night he made so much noise in the street that he was arrested and put in jail for a week.
When Pap got out of jail, the new judge still thought he could help him.
He took Pap into his own home, fed him, and gave him new clothes.
Pap cried and promised that he would become a better man.
The judge and his family believed him, but after a couple of days, my father traded his new coat for whiskey and got drunk again.
He fell off the judge's porch and broke his arm in two places.
After that, the judge stopped trying to help Pap.
I still lived at the Widow Douglas' house, and I still went to school.
But when Pap's arm was healed, he started chasing me again and demanding money.
If I didn't have any, he'd hit me.
So I started to borrow money from Judge Thatcher and give it to Pap.
Then he'd buy whiskey, get drunk, and be sent to jail for a few days. This went on for a while.
Finally, one day in the spring, Pap grabbed me and took me up the river in a small boat.
We landed at a place where there were no houses—just an old log hut hidden in the woods.
Pap kept me with him all the time, and I never got a chance to run away.
He always locked the door and he put the key under his head when he slept.
We fished and hunted, and that was how we got food.
Sometimes Pap locked me in the cabin and traveled down the river to a store.
There he traded our fish and the animals we killed for whiskey.
I began to enjoy my new lazy life with no books or studying.
Two months went by and my clothes were all dirty rags again.
I couldn't understand how I'd ever liked my life at the widow's house, where I had to wash, eat off a plate, and go to bed at a regular time.
But Pap's behavior became worse. He beat me so much that I had bruises all over me.
One time he went away and left me locked up for three days.
I made up my mind that I would have to get away from him. But how?
There was no way out of that cabin.
The window wasn't big enough for even a dog to go through, the chimney was too narrow, and the door was solid oak.
But on one wall of the cabin a blanket was nailed up to keep out the wind.
I searched the cabin for a useful tool and finally found one lying on a roof beam. It was an old rusty saw.
While Pap was away, I began to saw at a log in the wall that was hidden by the blanket.
I was almost finished sawing through the log when Pap came back again.
Pap made me go to the boat and get the things he had bought.
There was a twenty-kilogram sack of cornmeal, a big piece of bacon, and a fifteen-liter jug of whiskey.
I carried the supplies to the cabin, and then I sat down on the bow of the boat to rest.
I decided that when Pap got drunk and fell asleep I would finish sawing a hole in the cabin and run away.
I'd take Pap's gun and I would live by hunting and fishing.
I'd go so far away that neither Pap nor the Widow Douglas would ever find me.
But luck didn't go my way. Instead of falling asleep after drinking his whiskey, Pap had terrible visions.
He thought that snakes were crawling all over him and biting him.
His eyes were wild and he grabbed at the air with his hands, knocking things over.
Later in the night, he thought I was the angel of death.
He chased me around the cabin with a knife until he collapsed, but in the morning, he couldn't remember anything he'd done.
Pap told me to go down to the river and see if we had caught any fish on our lines.
I saw that the water was rising, and many logs and branches were floating down the river.
And then I saw a big canoe riding the waves like a duck. No one was in it.
I waded right into the water to get it, and then I paddled it back to shore and hid it under some willow branches.
By the time Pap came down to the river, I was taking five catfish off the fishing lines.
We had breakfast, and then we took a rest. I was still thinking about my escape.
I needed to make sure that Pap and the Widow Douglas wouldn't try to bring me back. And then I thought of a way.
Later that day, Pap and I saw nine logs joined together—part of a raft—coming down the river.
We went out in our rowboat and towed them ashore.
Then Pap locked me in the cabin and went off in the rowboat, towing the logs to sell them.
I didn't think he'd be back until the next morning.
I finished sawing through my hidden log until I could push out a piece and escape through the hole.
First I took the big sack of cornmeal down to the canoe, pushed the willow branches aside, and put the sack in the canoe.
Then I went back and forth, bringing other things from the cabin: the bacon, the jug of whiskey, and the coffee and sugar.
I also took a tin cup, two blankets, matches, and fishing lines.
I cleaned out that cabin. Last of all I took the gun.
The next thing I did was to go hunting and shoot a wild pig.
I brought its body back to the cabin.
Then I took the ax from our woodpile and smashed in the cabin door.
I smeared some of the pig's blood on the floor of the cabin and on the ax.
I pulled a few hairs out of my head and left them sticking to the bloody ax.
I got rid of the pig by carrying it down to the river and throwing it into the water.
Next I loaded a sack with stones.
Starting at the cabin, I dragged the sack through the dirt so that it left a trail all the way down to the river.
I dumped the sack into the water and it sank.
Then I thought of one more thing I could do.
I took the sack of cornmeal from the canoe up to the cabin, where I cut a small hole in the bottom.
I dragged it to a nearby lake, and as I walked, I left a trail of cornmeal coming out of the hole in the bag.
When I got to the lake, I tied up the bottom of the sack with string, so the cornmeal wouldn't leak anymore.
Then I carried the bag back to the canoe and climbed in.
I paddled a little way down the river to where some willows hung over the bank.
By now it was getting dark. I ate some food and rested and thought about my plan.
I hoped I had made it look as if robbers had come to the cabin, broken down the door, killed me with an ax,
and then dragged my body down to the water.
People might look for my body in the river, but they'd soon give up.
If they decided to chase the robbers, they'd follow the trail of grain to the lake. Meanwhile I would get away.
No one would follow me; I could go anywhere on the Mississippi River I wanted.
I decided I would go to Jackson's Island, out in the middle of the river.
I knew it well, and nobody ever went there.
At night I would be able to paddle over to St. Petersburg and creep around to get the things I needed.
I was very tired, and I soon fell asleep.
When I woke up, I didn't know where I was for a minute.
I sat up and looked around, feeling a little scared.
Then I remembered: I was hiding under some willows on the riverbank with the canoe.
I looked out across the Mississippi River; it was so wide. The other bank seemed far, far away.
The moon was so bright I could have counted the logs that floated on the river.
Everything was quiet and it looked late. It even smelled late, if you know what I mean.
I yawned and stretched and started to untie the canoe when I heard the sound of oars.
Soon I saw a rowboat coming toward me.
When it got closer, I saw that it was Pap, but he didn't see me because it was dark and I was hidden by the willow bushes.
As soon as he was on shore, I started paddling as fast as I could to the middle of the river.
Then I lay down in the bottom of the canoe and just let it float downstream.
I listened to the sounds that carried over the water.
I could even hear men talking on the ferry dock by the shore.
As I floated farther, their voices faded slowly away.
Finally, I sat up and saw by the moonlight that I had come to Jackson's Island.
I landed the canoe in a hollow on the shore of the island and covered it with willow branches so that no one could see it.
As morning approached, the sky turned gray, and I went into the woods and had a nap.
When I woke up, the sun was up high.
I lay in the cool shade of the trees and felt rested and comfortable.
A little breeze was blowing in the branches, and a couple of squirrels were chattering up there. I fell asleep again.
I was awakened by a loud boom from the river.
I peeked out from the trees and saw a ferryboat full of people out in the middle of the river.
They were firing a cannon over the water, and I knew why they were doing it.
They thought I was dead and they were trying to make my body rise up to the surface of the water.
I went down to the riverbank and hid behind a log.
As the ferryboat came closer to Jackson's Island, I looked through a hole in the log.
I could see Pap, Judge Thatcher, Tom Sawyer, and lots of other people I knew from St. Petersburg. Everyone was talking about my murder.
Then the captain said, "Maybe his body washed ashore and got tangled in the brush at the water's edge. I hope so, anyway."
They all crowded up to the front of the boat and leaned over the rails, watching.
I could see them clearly, but they couldn't see me.
The boat floated on and went out of sight.
I heard the cannon boom now and then, further and further off.
After a while, I heard the boat on the other side of the island.
It had turned around, and the people were going back to St. Petersburg.
Now I guessed that they had stopped looking for me.
I got my supplies out of the canoe and made a nice camp in the woods.
I made a tent out of my blankets to keep my things out of the rain.
I caught a catfish, and around sunset, I lit a campfire and had supper.
Then I set out a fishing line to catch some fish for breakfast.
When the night became dark, I sat by my campfire, and as it got later, I felt lonely.
I went down to the riverbank and listened to the river and counted the logs and rafts and stars. Finally, I went to bed.
The next three days were exactly the same, but on the fourth day, I explored the island.
It belonged to me and I wanted to know all about it.
I took my gun just in case I saw animals I could kill for food.
I found lots of ripe strawberries, green summer grapes, and unripe raspberries I could eat later on.
Then I almost stepped on a large snake.
It slid off through the grass and flowers, and I ran after it, trying to shoot it.
Suddenly I leaped onto the ashes of a campfire that was still smoking.
My heart was beating so hard it was jumping out of my chest.
I backed away as fast as I could, and then I ran.
Every time I saw a bush, I thought it was a man.
When I got back to camp, I hid all my supplies back in my canoe.
I put out my campfire and climbed a tree.
I couldn't stay up there forever, so finally I came down, but I stayed in the thick woods.
By nighttime I was very hungry, but I was afraid to stay on the island.
So I paddled my canoe over to the Illinois shore.
I went into the woods there and had a meal of berries and the fish left over from my breakfast.
I had just decided I would stay there all night when I heard horses coming, and then I heard men's voices.
I was afraid they would see me, so I jumped into my canoe and paddled back to Jackson's Island.
I tied up the canoe in its usual place and decided to sleep in it, but I couldn't sleep much.
Every time I woke up, I thought somebody had me by the neck.
Finally I decided that I couldn't live this way.
I had to search until I found out who was on Jackson's Island with me.
I paddled my canoe along the shore of the island, keeping close to land.
The moon shone almost as bright as day, but I didn't see anything moving on the shore.
When I got to the other end of the island, I landed the canoe.
By now it was almost morning. With my gun in my hand, I moved quietly through the woods to the place where I had seen the campfire ashes.
After a little while, I saw the light of a campfire through the trees.
As I crept closer, I saw a man lying on the ground with a blanket over him. It was Miss Watson's black slave Jim!
I called out, "Hi, Jim!" and skipped out of the trees.
He jumped up and stared at me wildly as if I were a ghost.
Then he moaned, "Don't hurt me! I've never harmed a ghost.
You get right back in that river again!"
I quickly made Jim understand that I wasn't dead and that I was very glad to see him.
I told him that I trusted him not to tell anyone where I was.
Jim told me that he'd been on the island since the night after I was killed, with nothing to eat but berries.
Now he was very hungry. We walked together to my canoe.
I got out my cornmeal, bacon and coffee, a frying pan, and a coffeepot.
While Jim got a fire going and cooked bacon and cornmeal, I caught a catfish.
Jim cleaned and fried it, and we had a delicious breakfast. Then we lay in the grass, relaxing.
After a while, Jim asked who had been killed in that cabin, if it wasn't me.
I told him the whole story of how I tricked everyone.
Then I asked him why he was camping on the island.
Jim looked very uneasy and didn't say anything for a minute.
Then he said, "You won't tell anyone about me, will you?"
I promised I wouldn't.
"Well, Huck—I ran away."
I was shocked. Black slaves belonged to their owners.
It was against the law for slaves to run away.
But I would never break my promise to Jim, and I told him so.
Then Jim explained why he had run away from Miss Watson.
"Miss Watson promised that she wouldn't sell me, but I saw a slave trader at her house recently, and I began to get uneasy.
One night I went past the house, and I heard Miss Watson tell the Widow Douglas that she was going to sell me for eight hundred dollars.
I didn't wait to hear any more—I just ran away down to the river.
I hid in a shack until morning. I thought maybe I could steal a rowboat, but there were people around all the time.
I heard your Pap and other people talking about how you'd been murdered.
I was very sorry to hear it, Huck.
I was hungry, but I wasn't afraid.
I knew Miss Watson and the widow were going to be out all day, so they wouldn't notice that I was gone until evening.
When it got dark, I walked along the river until I came to a place with no houses.
I realized that if I stole a boat, people would know I'd taken it.
What I wanted was a raft of those logs that float down the river.
When I saw one, I swam out to it, climbed on, and lay down on the wood.
The river was moving fast, and I expected to be forty kilometers away by morning.
But I didn't have good luck. Men with lanterns in their boats came after me, looking for me.
When one of them got so close that he would see me, I slid off the raft and swam to this island.
I decided to stay here until the men stopped looking for me.
I had some matches in my hat where they wouldn't get wet, so I could make a fire. I was all right."
Just then some young birds came along, flying short little distances and landing often.
Jim said it was a sign that it was going to rain.
Jim knew lots of signs. For instance, he said you shouldn't count the things you are going to cook for dinner, because that will bring bad luck.
And you shouldn't shake a tablecloth after sundown.
"Jim, it seems as if all the signs you know are about bad luck," I said. "Don't you know any good luck signs?"
"Very few," he replied. "Why do you need to know if good luck is coming? Do you need to keep it away?"
Then he told me that if a man had hairy arms and a hairy chest, it meant he was going to be rich someday.
Jim had hair on his arms and chest, so I asked him if he was rich.
"Yes, I am, now that I think of it," he said.
"I own myself, and I'm worth eight hundred dollars, but I wish I had the money."
Jim and I went to look more closely at a hill I'd seen when I first explored the island.
It was steep and covered with bushes, so it was a hard climb.
Almost at the top, we found a rock cave big enough for Jim to stand up in.
Jim suggested that we put all our gear in the cave and then hide the canoe among the willow branches on the shore.
"If anyone comes to the island," he said, "we can hide in the cave quickly and then no one will ever find us.
Besides," he reminded me, "the little birds said it's going to rain, and the cave will keep our things dry."
I thought this was a good idea, so we did it.
Then we built a fire outside the cave and cooked a fish and cornbread dinner.
We spread our blankets inside the cave for a carpet, and while we were eating dinner in there, it began to thunder and lightning.
The wind howled and the rain poured down, just as Jim had predicted.
"Jim, this is nice," I said. "I wouldn't want to be anywhere but here."
The river kept rising for over a week and finally flooded the banks.
The lower parts of the island were under a meter of water, and we paddled around them in our canoe.
At night, when no one could see us, we went out on the river.
One night, we caught a big lumber raft made of pine logs and hid it by the shore.
Another night, just before dawn, we saw a whole house floating down the river.
At daybreak, we paddled over to it and looked in the window.
We could see some furniture, some clothes hanging, and something that looked like a man lying on the floor.
We called to him, but he didn't move.
"He's not asleep," Jim said. "He's dead. You stay here, and I'll climb in and have a look."
After a minute, he called back to me to say that the man had been shot in the back.
He pulled some rags over him to hide him, and then he let me come in.
I didn't look at the dead man at all.
There were men's and women's clothes in the house, and useful things like candles and candlesticks, a tin cup, and fishing line and hooks.
By the time we piled everything in the canoe, the house had floated a long way down the river.
It took a lot of paddling to get back to the island.
After we got to shore, we carried everything back to our cave.
After breakfast, I wanted to talk about the dead man and how he came to be killed, but Jim didn't want to.
He said it would bring bad luck, and the dead man might even come back and haunt us.
But I couldn't help thinking about him, wondering who he was and why he was murdered.
We looked at the clothes we had taken and found eight dollars in coins sewed into the lining of the coat.
I told Jim that he was wrong to say we'd have bad luck because now we were having good luck.
But Jim just said that the bad luck was still coming. And he was sure right.
A few days later, I went into the cave while Jim was outside.
I found a rattlesnake in there and killed it.
I thought it would be funny to leave the snake curled up on Jim's bed as if it were still alive.
When bedtime came, Jim climbed into bed and gave a yell.
The dead snake's mate had crawled in beside it and had bitten Jim on the foot! I killed it with a stick.
Jim believed in old-fashioned ways to save yourself from a snake's poison.
He said I had to roast the snake and give him a piece of it to eat.
He also told me to make a bracelet from the snake's rattles and tie it around his wrist.
I did that too. I also brought him the whiskey jug to drink from because he was thirsty.
Jim's foot and leg swelled up and stayed that way for four days.
On the fifth day, he began to feel better and the swelling went down.
But Jim warned me, "Handling a snakeskin brings so much bad luck that we probably haven't come to the end of it yet."
The days passed by and the river went down to its normal level again.
I was beginning to get tired of staying on the island.
I wanted to go back to our town and see what was going on.
Jim told me that I should go at night and be very careful.
Then he got the idea that I should dress up as a girl.
I put on a dress and a sunbonnet that we had taken from the floating house.
Then he made me practice walking like a girl.
He said I had to stop lifting up my dress to get things out of my pants pocket.
I paddled over to town in the canoe and tied it up.
Nearby a light was shining in a shabby little house.
I peeked in the window and saw a middle-aged woman sitting at a table.
I thought I knew everyone in town, but I'd never seen this woman before. I knocked on the door.
The woman invited me into her house and said, "Take a chair."
I sat down. She looked at me closely and asked my name.
"Sarah Williams," I answered.
Then she asked where I was from, and I told her I came from Hookerville, about ten kilometers away.
I said that my mother was sick and I had come to look for my uncle, Abner Moore.
She explained that she had been living in the town for only two weeks and didn't know my uncle.
She invited me to stay the night, but I said that I would just rest for a while and then leave.
Then she began to talk about the recent murder in St. Petersburg.
"Who killed Huckleberry Finn?" I asked.
"Some people think it was his father," she said, "and some people think it was Jim, a runaway slave.
There's a reward for catching the slave—three hundred dollars.
After the boy was murdered, old Finn came into town.
He cried and begged Judge Thatcher for some money so he could hunt for the slave.
The last time anyone saw him, he was with some very tough-looking men.
Some people think old Finn killed his son so that he could get his money, and that he'll come back for it."
"Does that mean they've stopped hunting for the slave?" I asked.
"Oh no," she said. "Some people still think Jim did it.
And they would like that three hundred dollar reward.
My husband and his friends are out looking for Jim right now.
I told my husband he should look on Jackson's Island.
I've seen smoke over there at night, and I think the slave is hiding there."
I felt very nervous when she said this.
I needed something to do so that she would not see how scared I was.
I saw some sewing supplies sitting on the table beside me.
I picked up a needle from the table and tried to thread it, but I didn't do a good job.
The woman watched me, and finally she said, "What's your real name? Is it Bill? Tom?"
I started to shake and didn't know what to say.
But she said kindly, "I think you are a poor runaway boy who has been treated badly.
I'll keep your secret, and I'll give you some food for your journey, but I don't think you should try to pretend to be a girl.
When you thread a needle, you are supposed to hold the needle still and bring the thread to it.
You brought the needle to the thread, and no girl would do that."
I thanked the woman and left her house as quickly as I could, running back to the canoe.
I paddled over to the island and climbed up to our cave.
"Jim, wake up!" I cried. "We have to leave right away. They're after us!"
It was about one in the morning by the time we left the island.
We were on the big raft we had found a few days before.
We had piled all our supplies and our canoe on it.
When daylight came, we tied the raft up on the riverbank and hid it with branches.
Then we lay in the shade all day and watched the big steamboats going up and down the river.
I wondered if the men had found our campsite yet.
Just before we left, I had built a campfire to fool them.
I hoped they had sat by it all night, waiting for Jim to come back.
We spent every night on our raft. Jim used some planks to make a little hut for us in the middle of the raft.
The hut had a raised floor, and in the middle, we made a pit and filled it with earth. Here we could build a fire if we got cold.
Every night we traveled, floating downriver with the current.
On the fifth night, we passed the great city of St. Louis, which looked like the whole world lit up.
It was completely silent though—all the people were asleep.
We had lots of food to eat.
In the early morning, before the sun came up, I would sneak ashore into a farmer's field and take a watermelon or some corn.
Every evening I would go into a town to buy a little cornmeal or bacon. Sometimes I shot a duck.
One night there was a big thunderstorm. We stayed inside the hut as the rain poured down on our raft.
Flashes of lightning lit up the river, and suddenly I saw something ahead.
It was a wrecked steamboat caught on a rock.
I wanted to go aboard and have a look around, but Jim was against it.
"Maybe there's someone on board," he said.
"No one will be on a wreck like that," I argued. "And we might find some supplies on board."
We tied our raft up to the boat, and I explored it while Jim waited by the raft.
Suddenly I heard a frightened voice crying, "Oh, please don't, boys. I swear I will never tell."
I peeked into a cabin on the wrecked steamboat to see what was going on.
A man was lying on the floor, tied up, and two other men were standing over him.
One had a lantern and the other had a gun.
They were arguing about whether or not to shoot the man on the floor.
Finally they decided that they would just leave him tied up on the wreck.
When it slid off the rock and sank, he would drown.
Meanwhile, they were going to get in their rowboat and row away.
I ran back to Jim, very scared. I whispered, "Quick, Jim, there are murderers on this boat!
We have to find the rowboat and cut it loose, so they can't get away. Then we'll get on our raft—"
But Jim interrupted me. "Huck, we don't have a raft! It broke loose and floated away!"
We were trapped on a wreck with wicked men and no way to get off!
I realized that we had to find that rowboat right away, for ourselves.
Jim and I felt along the sides of the wreck in the dark, until finally we found the boat.
We were about to jump into it when a door opened and the man with the lantern stepped outside.
We kept still and he didn't see us as he threw a big bag into the boat.
Both men got into the rowboat, and one man said to the other, "All ready—shove off."
Then the second man said, "Wait a minute—did you go through his pockets?"
"No, I didn't," replied the first.
The two men decided to go back on the wreck and see if the tied-up man had any money they could take.
The minute they went back inside, Jim and I jumped into the rowboat.
I cut the rope with my knife and the river current began to carry us away.
We didn't touch the oars, and we didn't speak or whisper. We hardly dared to breathe.
When we were about three hundred meters downstream, Jim took the oars and began to row.
I started to worry about the robbers on the wreck.
Even though they were bad men, I didn't want to just leave them to drown.
The storm blew up again, and as the lightning flashed, we searched for our raft in the water.
Finally we found it. Just then we saw a light on the shore too.
"Jim," I said, "you keep floating on the raft.
Shine a lantern for me so I can find you.
I'm going to take the boat and go to that light.
I want to get help for the men on the wreck."
As I got close to shore, I saw that the light came from a ferryboat sitting on the water.
I found the captain on board, asleep. I woke him up and told him a sad story that I made up.
"Pap and Ma'am and my sister . . ." I began, and then I started to cry.
"Don't cry, now," he said. "Everything will be all right. What's the trouble?"
I said that my family had tried to cross the river late at night, but we had lost our oars.
Floating helplessly down the river, our boat had hit the wrecked steamboat.
We all climbed onto the wreck, but we realized it would soon sink.
I was the only one who could swim, so my dad said I must swim to shore and get help.
And now here I was, begging the captain to take his boat and help them.
The captain promised he would get his crew right away, and they would take the ferry out to the wreck.
In the meantime, he directed me to an inn nearby where I could get warm and dry.
But as soon as he left me, I got into the rowboat and rowed out onto the river to find Jim and the raft.
I felt good about trying to save the gang from drowning.
I only wished there was some way the Widow Douglas could know what I had done.
When I rowed past the wreck again, I saw that it was now mostly underwater.
I called out, but no one answered. Then I realized that it was too late to save the men.
I felt sad. It seemed like a long, long time before I saw the light on the raft.
It was almost morning when I finally caught up with Jim.
We found an island, sank the rowboat, and hid the raft on shore. Then we slept until the afternoon.
When we woke up, we looked at all the things the gang had stolen from the wrecked boat.
We found boots, blankets, clothes, and lots of books.
We spent most of the day lying under the trees, talking.
Then I read to Jim from a book about kings and dukes, and how fancy their clothes were,
and how they called each other "Your Majesty" and "Your Grace."
Jim was very interested. He asked me how much a king earned.
"Why, they can have a thousand dollars a month, if they want it," I said.
"They can have anything they want—everything belongs to them."
"What do they have to do to get it?" Jim asked.
"They don't have to do anything," I replied.
"They just sit around—except maybe when there's a war, then they go to the war."
Jim and I figured out that in three more days we would come to the town of Cairo, where the Ohio River joins the Mississippi.
There we could sell our raft and buy tickets for a steamboat going up the Ohio River.
It would take us to the North, where there was no slavery, and where Jim would be safe.
The next night, a fog rolled in. We looked for a place on the riverbank to tie up our raft.
I went ahead in the canoe with the raft's towline.
I looped the line around a small tree and tied it tight, but the raft tore the tree out by the roots and kept on going.
Now I was alone in the canoe, surrounded by a thick white blanket of fog.
After a time, I heard a voice yelling.
I paddled as fast as I could toward the sound, but when I heard the voice again, it seemed to be coming from another direction.
I paddled some more. At last I was so tired that I fell asleep in the canoe.
When I woke up, the fog had lifted.
Ahead of me, I saw the raft, and there was Jim, asleep.
I got on the raft and stretched out beside him.
I said, "Hey, Jim, have you been asleep?"
"Is that really you, Huck?" Jim exclaimed. "I thought you had drowned for sure!"
I decided to play a joke on Jim.
I told him that I'd been on the raft all along and that he had dreamed everything that happened in the fog.
He said that if it was a dream, everything in it must mean something.
The riverbank with the trees, he explained, was a man trying to help us, but the river current that pulled the raft away was a man trying to harm us.
The fog meant all kinds of troubles that we'd have to steer away from.
"And what do these things stand for?" I said, pointing to the leaves and trash that had collected on the raft in the fog.
Jim looked at them for a long time, and then he said slowly, "I fell asleep because I was so tired from calling for you.
I thought you were dead, and my heart was almost broken.
When I woke up and saw you alive, I was full of joy.
But you were only thinking about how you could make a fool of me with a lie.
So what that trash stands for is people who make fun of their friends."
I felt ashamed, and I told Jim I was sorry.
I never played any mean tricks on him again.
The next night, as we floated down the river, we talked again about the town of Cairo.
I was worried we might pass it in the dark.
Jim said that if we found Cairo, he'd soon be a free man, but if we missed it, we'd still be in the South, where black people are slaves.
He talked about the things he would do when he reached the North.
He'd get a job and save all his money.
Then he would buy his wife from the man who owned her, so they could live together again.
When we saw lights ahead, we tied up the raft on the riverbank.
Then I took the canoe and paddled toward the town.
I came to a man in a rowboat, and I asked him if the town ahead was Cairo. He told me it wasn't.
Jim was very disappointed, but we set out on the raft again.
Later that night we passed another town that was on high ground.
We knew there was no high ground around Cairo, so we kept going.
When daylight came, we could see the clear water of the Ohio River near the shoreline,
so we knew we had passed the place where the clear Ohio and the muddy Mississippi join together.
"Maybe we passed by Cairo that night in the fog," I said.
"Let's not talk about it, Huck," he said. "It's just bad luck.
I always thought that snakeskin wasn't done with us yet."
"I'm so sorry I touched it, Jim!" I said.
He told me not to blame myself.
Now we had to turn around and go back upriver.
The floating raft couldn't go upriver, so we would have to go in the canoe.
We slept all day on the shore under the trees, but when we went back to the raft in the evening, the canoe was gone!
Neither of us said a word for a long while.
We both thought it was the snakeskin bringing us more bad luck.
Finally, we decided that we would have to keep going downriver on the raft.
Maybe we'd come to a town where we could buy another canoe.
We set off into the night, but the snakeskin wasn't finished with its work yet.
The fog closed in around us. We could hear a big steamboat coming in the other direction, with its huge stern wheel churning and pounding.
We lit our lantern, but the steamboat was headed right for us.
Jim jumped overboard off one side of the raft, and I jumped off the other.
The steamboat tore into our raft and kept going.
When I came to the surface, I called to Jim, but I couldn't hear any answer.
Finally I swam to shore. Then I started walking and I came to a big log house.
Suddenly a pack of dogs jumped out of the darkness, howling and barking at me.
The dogs kept barking at me and I was afraid to move.
Then a man called out of the window of the house, "Calm down, boys! Who's there?"
"It's me," I said.
"Who's me?" asked the voice.
"George Jackson, sir. I'm only a boy."
"What do you want?"
"I don't want anything, sir. I only want to pass by the house, but the dogs won't let me."
"Why are you prowling around here at this time of night, huh?" he asked.
"I wasn't prowling around, sir." I began to make up a story in my head to tell him. "I fell overboard off a steamboat."
"Look here, if you're telling the truth, you needn't be afraid," said the man in a kinder voice.
"Nobody will hurt you." Then he shouted, "Bob and Tom, wake up and fetch the guns!"
I heard more people moving around in the house.
Then the man called out to me again.
"George Jackson, do you know the Shepherdsons?"
"No sir," I said truthfully. "I never heard of them."
"Well, then, walk forward slowly and push the door open, just enough to squeeze in."
I took one slow step at a time.
As I got close to the front door, I heard the people inside unlocking it. I pushed it and stepped inside.
By candlelight I could see three big men, all with guns pointed at me.
The oldest was about sixty; the other two were young men.
Behind them were an old lady and two younger women.
As soon as I was inside, the old gentleman locked the door again.
Then all of us went into the parlor.
They all took a good look at me and decided that I didn't look like a Shepherdson.
The old lady noticed that I was all wet.
She told her servant girl to get me some food and to wake up Buck.
Buck came down a few minutes later, rubbing his eyes.
He looked to be about 13—my age.
Buck took me up to his room where he gave me some dry clothes.
He told me about a rabbit he had caught in the woods.
Then he asked me where Moses was when the candle went out.
I said I didn't know, and he said I should guess.
"How can I guess," I said, "when I never heard of it before?"
Finally he said, "He was in the dark!"
"Well, if you knew where he was, why did you ask me?" I said.
"It's a riddle," he said. Then he grinned at me.
"Are you going to stay here a while? I hope so.
I have a dog and we can go down to the river and have great times."
Still talking in this friendly way, he took me down to dinner.
It was the best food I had ever tasted: cornbread and butter and beef and buttermilk.
All the family members—their name was Grangerford, I soon found out—asked me questions.
I told them I came from Arkansas, that my mother and brother and sisters were all dead,
and that my father had drowned when we both fell off the steamboat, so I had no family.
They said that I could have a home with them as long as I wanted.
The Grangerfords lived in a beautiful house with lots of rooms.
Everything was kept clean and polished by all their black servants.
They had a clock on the mantel, with a china cat and dog on either side.
They had many books and lots of pictures on the walls.
Colonel Grangerford, the older man, treated his family kindly, and they loved him.
He and his two grown-up sons were handsome men and very well dressed.
His wife was a sweet-faced kind lady.
The two daughters were Miss Charlotte, who was proud, and Miss Sophia, who was quiet and gentle.
I found out that the family used to be larger, but a daughter had died, and three sons had been killed.
One day Buck and I were walking in the woods when we heard a horse coming.
"Quick, hide!" Buck said. We hid behind a tree and saw a handsome young horseman with a gun.
I later found out his name was Harney, and he was one of the Shepherdsons.
Suddenly Buck fired his gun, right by my ear, and Harney's hat flew off his head.
Then we both ran through the woods and didn't stop until we got back to the house.
Colonel Grangerford scolded Buck for shooting from behind a tree.
"But that's what the Shepherdsons do," Buck replied.
I noticed that Miss Sophia looked very pale until she heard that Harney Shepherdson wasn't hurt.
When Buck and I were by ourselves, I asked him why he wanted to hurt Harney Shepherdson.
"What did he do to you?" I asked.
"He never did anything to me," Buck answered.
"Well, why did you want to shoot at him?" I asked.
Then Buck told me that there was a feud between the Grangerfords and the Shepherdsons.
I had never heard this word before, so he explained that long ago, a man in one family had fought with a man in the other family, and killed him.
Then the dead man's brother shot the first man.
Then all the brothers and cousins got into the fight, too.
The feud had started more than thirty years ago.
No one could remember who had started the first fight, or what it was about. But the feud went on.
I asked Buck whether any Grangerfords and Shepherdsons had been killed in the past few months.
"Oh, yes," he replied calmly, "one of ours and one of theirs. We have a lot of funerals."
He went on to tell me that both his brothers and his father had been wounded in battles with the Shepherdsons.
On Sunday, I went to church with the Grangerfords.
The sermon was about brotherly love, but all the Grangerford men had their guns with them, and so did the Shepherdson men.
It was the strangest church service I had ever attended.
Later that afternoon, when I was going upstairs to my room, Miss Sophia came out of her room.
She told me in a whisper that she had forgotten her Bible in the church.
"Would you please go to the church and get it for me?" she said.
Then she added, "Please don't tell anyone."
I found the book, but it seemed odd that Miss Sophia was so nervous about a Bible, so I shook it to see if anything was inside.
A note fluttered out that said, "Two-thirty."
I tucked the note back in the Bible and, when I returned, gave the book to Miss Sophia without saying anything.
She gave me a hug and told me I was the best boy in the world.
Later I decided to go for a walk by the river.
I soon noticed that one of the house slaves, a man named Jack, was following me.
He asked me if I'd like to go down to the swamp and see some snakes.
I thought this was strange, but I agreed and followed him into the swamp.
We were ankle-deep in water for a while, and then we came to a dry place.
Jack said that I should go ahead while he went back to the house.
I took a few steps, pushing aside some vines, and there was Jim! I was so happy to see him.
Jim explained that he had managed to swim to shore a little while after I did.
When he saw me go into the house, he hid in the woods nearby.
The next day, he went up to some of the Grangerfords' slaves working in the fields and asked for their help.
They showed him a hiding place in the swamp.
And then Jim told me the best news of all.
The raft hadn't been completely destroyed by the steamboat.
He'd been repairing it, and it would be ready for travel in a couple of days.
When I woke up the next morning, the house was strangely quiet.
I went downstairs and Jack told me the terrible news.
Miss Sophia had run away to marry Harney Shepherdson.
The Grangerford women had gone to a relative's house to get more help, while Colonel Grangerford and his three sons had rode off with their guns.
They intended to kill Harney and bring Miss Sophia back.
I ran down the road after them as fast as I could, and before long I heard shooting.
I snuck through the trees until I came to the riverbank near a store that sold supplies to people traveling on the river.
Men were shooting at each other along the shore and from inside the store.
I could see Buck and an older boy who was his cousin hiding behind a big woodpile.
It was too dangerous to stay where I was, so I climbed a tree and hid there.
I saw several men shot dead on both sides, and then the Shepherdson men rode away.
I called out to Buck from the tree.
Crying and cursing the Shepherdsons, he told me that his father and both his older brothers had been killed.
I asked Buck what had happened to Harney and Miss Sophia, and he said they had gotten away.
He asked me to stay in the tree and watch for the Shepherdsons to ride back, and I said I would.
But suddenly gunfire broke out again. The Shepherdsons had circled back and snuck up on Buck and his cousin.
What happened next made me feel so sick I almost fell out of the tree.
I still have nightmares about it. The Shepherdsons killed Buck and his cousin. Then they fled.
I was so scared that I waited until it was dark before I climbed down from the tree.
I never wanted to see the Grangerford house again.
I blamed myself because I had brought the note to Miss Sophia.
Maybe if she hadn't received it, she wouldn't have run away.
I ran back to the dry spot in the swamp to find Jim—but he wasn't there!
I scrambled down to the riverbank, yelling his name.
Then I heard a soft voice: "Is that you, Huck? Don't make any noise."
It was Jim's voice—and nothing had ever sounded so good to me.
I ran a little way along the bank until I came to the raft and scrambled aboard.
Jim and I hugged each other. Once again, he had thought I was dead.
Jack had told him about the gun battle, and that I hadn't come home.
"Let's just leave, Jim, as fast as we can," I said.
When we were about three kilometers down the river, I began to feel safer.
We hung up our lantern and ate some supper.
I was very happy to get away from the feud, and Jim was happy to get away from the swamp.
We agreed there was no home as good as our raft.
The farther south we traveled, the hotter the temperature was and the wider the river became.
At times, it was almost two kilometers from one shore to the other.
At night, we lay on our raft and looked at the stars.
Sometimes we saw a shooting star streaking across the sky.
One morning, as we were tying up the raft on the riverbank, I saw an old canoe.
I paddled it up a little creek to look for berries.
Suddenly I saw two men running toward the creek.
When they saw me, they begged me to rescue them.
Men and dogs were chasing them, they said.
I let them get aboard, and I paddled away as fast as I could until we got back to the raft.
Jim and I and our passengers traveled on the raft a little way down the river.
Then we tied up the raft on shore under some cottonwood trees, where all of us were hidden and safe.
One of the men looked about seventy years old.
He wore a battered hat, ragged blue jeans stuffed into his boots, and an old blue coat with brass buttons.
The other man was probably about thirty years old, but his clothes were just as shabby as the old man's.
Both of them carried worn-out suitcases.
After we had breakfast and began to talk, I found out the two men didn't really know each other well.
They had met as they were running away from two different towns.
The old man said that he had been giving speeches in a small town.
He had charged the townspeople ten cents each to hear him warn against the evils of drinking alcohol.
Then someone saw him sneaking a drink himself, and the angry townspeople realized he was a fraud.
That's when they chased him out of town.
The young man had been in another town selling a medicine that was supposed to clean people's teeth.
When people used it, however, they found that it damaged their teeth.
That's why he had been chased out of town.
Jim and I listened in amazement as the two men described all the different kinds of work they had done.
The young man had been an actor, a printer, and a singing teacher.
The older man claimed that he had cured people of diseases just by placing his hands on their bodies.
"I think we should go into business together!" the younger man said eagerly to the older one.
But then his face became sad. "I can't believe that I have sunk so low in the world."
"Why, what's wrong with my company?" the older man said, sounding insulted.
"Nothing—it's what I deserve now," the younger man replied.
"But, at one time, my life was very different.
I trust all of you, so I will tell you my secret.
My father came from England—I am the Duke of Bridgewater!
But my wealth and title were stolen from me."
Jim and I felt very sorry for him.
He told us that if we wanted to make him feel better, we should call him "Your Grace" or "Your Lordship."
We should also serve him his meals. That was easy enough, so Jim and I did it.
By dinnertime, I could see that the older man wasn't too happy with all the attention we were giving the duke.
Finally, he said, "Can I trust you?"
We all assured him that he could. And then he said, "You see before you the poor wandering, unhappy king of France."
He began to cry, and Jim and I asked him how we could cheer him up.
He said that we should bow when we spoke to him and call him "Your Majesty." Jim and I said that we would.
The duke now looked annoyed. When the king noticed, he said, "It's not our fault that one of us was born a duke and the other a king.
Let's shake hands and be friends." The duke agreed.
The two men were curious about Jim and me.
They asked if Jim was a runaway slave.
"Goodness, no!" I said. "Would we be going south if he was a runaway?"
I made up a story, telling them that my father and brother had been killed in a steamboat accident and that Jim was now my slave.
I said that many people didn't believe me and thought Jim must be running away from his owner.
We traveled at night, I explained, so that we wouldn't have any trouble.
The duke and the king seemed to accept my story.
It rained hard that night.
Jim and I gave the two men our beds in the hut on the raft while we slept out in the rain, but it was so warm that we didn't mind.
In fact, we were treating the king and duke so well that they decided to keep traveling with us.
When we stopped along the river, they planned to go into towns and earn money.
The king began to teach the duke speeches from Shakespeare's plays.
He said they could charge people money to see them acting.
He even had some shabby costumes in his suitcase.
I had already decided that the two men were liars and cheats, not royalty.
But I wanted peace on the raft, so I didn't say anything, even to Jim.
Living with Pap had taught me that when you are with difficult people, it is better to stay quiet.
The next evening, after we tied up the raft, I went into a nearby town with the king and the duke.
Nearly everyone was at an outdoor religious meeting, and the king immediately thought of a way to make money from it.
The king and I stood at the back of the crowd and listened for a while as the townspeople sang some hymns.
Then the preacher said that anyone who had sinned should come forward and promise to live a better life.
The king leaped up and ran to the front of the meeting.
He said that he had been a pirate in the Indian Ocean for thirty years.
Now he understood that this was a bad way to live.
"All I want now," he said, "is to go back to the ocean and tell all the other pirates to stop their evil ways and live a good life."
Then he began to cry with shame. Many people in the crowd believed him and began to cry too.
"Let's collect some money for him to help him do his good work!" yelled someone in the crowd.
The townspeople passed a hat around to collect money and gave all of it to the king. He hugged them and thanked them.
When we got back to the raft, we found that he had collected 87 dollars and 75 cents.
The duke had been busy in town too.
He had thought of a clever way that we could travel in the daytime.
He showed us a poster he had printed.
It said "Two-Hundred Dollar Reward" in big letters; underneath, it described a black slave who had escaped from a plantation near New Orleans.
If other boats on the river came too close to our raft, we could tie Jim up so it would look as if he was our prisoner.
Then we could show people the poster and tell them we were taking Jim south to New Orleans to get the reward.
For the next two days, as we continued south on the river, the king and the duke rehearsed their play on the raft.
The duke had two wooden swords in his suitcase, and the two men practiced a fight scene.
On the third day, we arrived at a place in Arkansas called Bricksville.
A circus would be putting on a show in the afternoon, and the town was crowded with people who had come from the countryside to see it.
The duke rented a hall where the play could be staged that evening.
He also got some posters printed, announcing the play, and walked around town handing them out.
The charge would be 25 cents for each adult and 10 cents for each child.
In the afternoon, I snuck under the edge of the tent to watch the circus.
I saw handsome men, and women who looked like queens, with glittering jewels all over their costumes.
They stood up on the backs of horses that galloped around and around the circus ring.
It was the most amazing sight I had ever seen.
That night, the king and duke put on their Shakespearean play, but only 12 people came.
They laughed through the whole play, which wasn't supposed to be funny.
Afterward, the duke said that the people of Arkansas were too stupid to appreciate Shakespeare.
"Tomorrow night," he said. "We'll give them the show they deserve—the Royal Nonesuch."
The duke got new posters printed with the name of the show and the new price: fifty cents.
At the bottom, the poster said, "No women and children admitted."
That evening, the theater was packed with men.
The duke stood in front of the crowd and announced, "You are about to see the most thrilling performance in the history of theater!"
Then the king hurried onto the stage on all fours.
He wore no clothes, and his skin was painted all over with stripes of different colors.
The crowd roared with laughter and clapped. The king hopped off the stage and the duke reappeared.
If they had enjoyed the show, he said, they should tell their friends to come the next night.
People in the audience shouted angrily, "Is the show over already? You charged us fifty cents for this?"
Then a tall man in the audience stood up and said, "Yes, we've been tricked, gentlemen, but we don't want the whole town laughing at us.
Let's leave here and tell all the other men in town to see the show.
Then we'll all be fools, and no one will be laughing at anyone else."
Everyone must have followed his advice because our theater was filled again the next night.
Once again, the king hopped around for a couple of minutes.
But on the third night, the people arriving at the theater were angry men who had already seen the show.
I watched them as they came inside and I saw that they were bringing rotten eggs and cabbages to throw at the stage.
I ran backstage and told the king and duke that they should get out of town at once.
We all ran back to the raft where Jim was waiting.
By the time the audience realized we were gone, we had started down the river.
We didn't light our lantern until we were ten kilometers south.
Then we had our supper on the raft, while the king and duke counted their earnings.
They had 465 dollars. I had never seen so much money.
After the king and the duke had fallen asleep in the hut on the raft, Jim said to me, "Do you think the duke and the king are rascals?"
"Yes, I do," I replied. "From the books I've read, I've learned that many kings are rascals."
"Then I hope we don't meet any more of them," said Jim. "These two are all I can stand."
I went to sleep while Jim kept watch.
He was supposed to wake me later so that I could take my turn to watch, but he let me sleep.
When I awoke, it was dawn. I saw Jim sitting with his head bent low, and I knew he was feeling sad.
I asked him if he was thinking about his wife and children.
"Yes, I am," he replied. "I miss them so much.
I'm afraid I'll never see my little Elizabeth and my little Johnny again."
I tried to comfort him. I was thinking that black slaves had all the same feelings as white people.
They loved their families just as much. I began to wonder how anyone could sell a man and separate him from his family.
The king and the duke wished they could stage the Royal Nonesuch again because they had made so much money.
But they were afraid news of their trick might have spread to other towns.
If it had, they would need to think of a new scam.
Meanwhile, they bought themselves fine new clothes at the next town we came to.
They even bought some new clean clothes for me.
They told me that it was easier to fool people if you looked rich and respectable, and they proved this to me the next day.
The king and the duke asked me to take them in our canoe to the nearest steamboat wharf.
There we could board a big steamboat. Then they could arrive at the next town as if they were very important people.
They said that I could pretend to be their servant, Adolphus.
I didn't like that name, but I was so excited to be riding on a steamboat for the first time in my life that I didn't object.
As we boarded the steamboat, the king started a conversation with a friendly and trusting young man.
"When I first saw you, I thought you might be Mr. Harvey Wilks," the young man said.
The king replied, "No, I am Alexander Blodgett—but who is Mr. Wilks?"
"Well, everyone in our town has been waiting for Harvey Wilks and his brother William—William can't hear or speak—to arrive from England.
They are coming to see their brother Peter, who lived in our town.
When Peter fell very ill a month ago, he wrote to them asking them to come, but I'm afraid Peter passed away yesterday."
"Didn't Peter have any other relatives?" asked the king.
"He did have a brother George, who lived nearby.
But George and his wife both died a few months ago, leaving three daughters."
Then the young man's face brightened. "But at least Peter left a letter for Harvey.
People in town say that the letter tells Harvey where Peter hid all his money.
Peter wanted to be sure that Harvey would share the money with George's three daughters because their father was a poor man."
"Why, what are the dear girls' names?" asked the king keenly.
"Mary Jane is the oldest—she's 19. Then there's Susan, who is 15, and Joanna, 14."
The king shook his head at the sadness of their young lives, and then continued his questioning: "Was Peter Wilks a wealthy man?"
"Oh, yes," replied the young man innocently.
"He owned several houses and land. People say he had three or four thousand dollars hidden away somewhere."
"Have Harvey and William Wilks ever come to visit before?"
"No," said the young man. "Everyone in town is very curious to meet them."
By the time we got off that steamboat, the king had found out everything there was to know about Peter Wilks.
The friendly young man was continuing south to New Orleans where he would board a ship to South America.
So there was no one to stop the king and the duke from pretending to be Harvey and William Wilks.
And that is just what they did.
The king and the duke walked from the steamboat wharf into the town.
I followed them, carrying their suitcases. There they met some men who had gathered to watch the steamboat arrive.
The king asked anxiously, "Can anyone tell me where Mr. Peter Wilks lives?"
"I'm very sorry, sir," said one of the men. "Peter Wilks has died."
The king grabbed the man and sobbed on his shoulder, "Oh no! Our poor brother!" Then the duke started crying too.
The townspeople gathered around and said how sorry they were.
Then they led us to a house where three girls were standing in a doorway.
The oldest girl—I knew she must be Mary Jane—was red-haired and beautiful.
She ran to hug the king, who she thought was her uncle Harvey.
The other two girls cried and hugged the duke, who they thought was their deaf uncle William.
I felt ashamed of these two liars and ashamed of myself for being with them.
Peter Wilks' funeral was going to be the next afternoon.
In the meantime, his coffin was in the parlor of his house.
I watched with disgust while the king prayed and cried beside the coffin.
Meanwhile, the duke, who was pretending to be William, just stood quietly and looked sad.
Mary Jane gave the king the letter that Peter Wilks had left.
He read it aloud. It said that Peter gave his own house and three thousand dollars to his three nieces.
He gave his tannery business, some other houses and land, and three thousand dollars to his brothers Harvey and William.
The letter also said where the money—six thousand dollars in gold coins—was hidden in the cellar.
Right away, the king and the duke said they would get the money.
They took me with them to the dark cellar and asked me to hold a candle.
They quickly found the bag of money, and their eyes shone with greed.
The two men counted the coins carefully to make sure it was all there.
Then we went upstairs, and they counted it again in front of everyone.
"My friends," said the king. "My poor brother has been very generous.
He left as much as he could to these poor lambs"—he meant the three girls—"but he wanted to leave something for us, his brothers.
However, I feel they need it more. Here, Mary Jane, Susan, and Joanna—take it all." The king handed the bag to Mary Jane.
Everyone said how generous he was. While the girls hugged and kissed him, I noticed that a tall man had come into the room.
The king noticed him and went over to shake his hand, but the man pulled his hand away angrily.
"Why Doctor Robinson," Mary Jane said, "don't you know this is my uncle's brother Harvey Wilks?"
"He's just pretending to be an Englishman," the doctor replied.
"He has the worst English accent I've ever heard.
I don't believe he is my good friend's brother, and I won't shake his hand."
Mary Jane was shocked, but the doctor continued, "I warn you not to trust these men.
They've learned all about your family somehow, and they have come here to cheat you."
But Mary Jane said to the doctor, "Here is my answer to you." She took the bag of money and gave it to the king.
"Take this six thousand dollars," she said, "and invest it for us. I trust you."
Doctor Robinson gave up and left the house.
That night, there was a big dinner for Peter Wilks' friends.
As a servant, I didn't get a chance to eat until after dinner had been served, but there was lots of food left over.
I was sitting in the kitchen eating when Joanna, the youngest sister, came in.
She was very curious about my life in England.
"Did you ever see the king of England?" she asked.
"Oh, yes," I answered. "He came to our church every week."
"But I thought he lived in London," Joanna said.
"Yes, he does."
"But don't you live in Sheffield?" she asked, with a puzzled look on her face.
Darn! I had forgotten that we were supposed to be from Sheffield.
I thought quickly. "Well, I meant he comes to our church in Sheffield in the summertime. He comes to swim in the sea."
"But Sheffield is nowhere near the sea," she said. "Are you just making this up?"
"No, not at all!" I said quickly.
But soon I made another mistake. Joanna asked me how servants were treated in England.
"Oh, very badly," I replied. "They're not allowed to go to circuses or theaters—or even to church."
"But you're a servant and you said you go to church," Joanna said. "I don't believe you."
Mary Jane and Susan came into the kitchen at that moment.
"What don't you believe?" asked Mary Jane.
"It isn't kind to speak that way to someone so far from home. You must apologize to Adolphus."
And Joanna did apologize to me, very sweetly.
At that moment, I knew that I couldn't let the king and the duke take their money.
I went up to bed early, but I couldn't sleep.
I had to think of a way to get the money back for the girls.
Everyone else was still downstairs, so I decided I would search the rooms of the king and the duke.
While I was looking in the king's room, I heard the two men coming up the stairs. I quickly hid under the bed.
They came in and shut the door. The duke said he thought they should take the money and leave town that very night.
"That doctor might make trouble for us."
But the king refused. "No, I want to stay and sell the houses and land that were left to us. We'll make even more money."
The duke finally agreed. "But I don't like our hiding place for the money," he said. "A servant might find it."
The two men got the bag from somewhere in the room.
I heard them making a rip in the mattress just above me, and they hid the money inside it.
Then they went back downstairs to join the other guests.
At that point, although I had no real plan, I quickly grabbed the bag of money.
I wanted to get away that very night.
I hoped to rejoin Jim so we could continue down the river.
Later, after the king and the duke had gone away, I would send all the money back to Mary Jane.
I waited until the house was quiet, except for the snores coming from the king's room.
I crept downstairs and passed by the parlor door.
One candle was burning in there, and I could see the coffin.
I tried to open the front door, but it was locked and I didn't have the key.
While I was thinking about what to do next, I heard someone coming down the stairs.
I hurried into the parlor. Where could I hide the money bag?
The coffin lid was partly open, so I shoved the bag in there.
I accidentally touched Peter's cold hands, which made me shiver.
I quickly hid behind the door just as Mary Jane came into the room.
She sat beside the coffin and cried softly.
Her back was to me, and I snuck out of the room.
I couldn't get out of the house now, so I went back up to bed.
I felt very worried, but if the money stayed where it was, everything would be all right.
I would run away tomorrow and go back to Jim.
When we were a hundred kilometers down the river, I could write a letter to Mary Jane and tell her the money was buried with her uncle.
But I didn't think things would go that smoothly.
What if someone at the funeral decided to take a last look at Peter and noticed the money bag?
Then the king and the duke would find a way to steal it from Mary Jane again.
All through the funeral the next morning, I was scared.
Would someone find the money bag in the coffin?
But no one did, and Peter Wilks was buried in the cemetery.
I just wished I could be sure the money was really in the coffin with him.
I worried that someone might have gone into the parlor late in the night and taken it.
Meanwhile, the king announced that he would be holding an auction of Peter Wilks' property in two days.
He and his brother had to get back to England, he said.
The lying scoundrel also said that he would take the sisters to England with him.
Poor Mary Jane and her sisters began to pack.
I knew he wouldn't be taking them anywhere, that he and the duke would run away as soon as the auction was over.
I longed to tell Mary Jane the truth, but I was afraid of what the king and the duke would do to me.
Then something even worse happened. Two slave traders arrived in town.
The king sold the family's black slaves to them.
He sold two sons to one trader and their mother to the other trader.
The slaves were very upset as they were being taken away.
Mary Jane and her sisters cried and cried.
Many people in town said that it was a terrible thing to separate a slave family this way.
They began to think that Harvey and William weren't as nice as they had thought.
The next morning, the king and the duke came up to the attic and shook me awake.
"Were you in my room last night or the night before?" the king demanded.
I understood at once that they knew the money bag was gone.
"Why no, Your Majesty!" I said.
"Did you see anyone else go in there?"
"Well, I might have seen the slaves go in there to clean up," I lied, thinking fast.
After that, the king and the duke believed that the slaves had stolen the money and they stopped searching for it.
I knew the black slaves were already far away, where the king couldn't harm them.
As I went downstairs for breakfast, I saw Mary Jane packing her trunk.
She looked so unhappy that I couldn't bear it any longer.
I decided to tell her the truth.
I told her how the king and the duke had met the young man on the boat and how,
after listening to him, they had decided to pretend to be Peter's brothers.
I told her they were thieves and liars.
She believed me and her eyes blazed with anger.
She wanted to have them arrested right away, but I asked her to wait until the next day.
I explained that I needed to get away first.
I couldn't tell her why, but said that I had to help another person who needed me.
I was pretty sure that when Mary Jane told the townspeople about the scoundrels, they would believe her.
But, in case she needed more proof, I told her she could write to the mayor of Bricksville
and tell him that the men who had staged the Royal Nonesuch were in her town.
The mayor would be happy to tell everyone that the two men were crooks.
"And there's one more thing," I said. "The bag of money."
"Well, those scoundrels have that," she said. "I was foolish, and I gave it to them."
"No, they don't have it," I said. "I took it from them to give to you.
I don't have it now, but I know where it is."
At that point, Mary Jane gave me a big hug, which made my face go red.
Mary Jane was so sweet that I didn't want to tell her I had put the money in her uncle's coffin.
So I said to her, "I'll write it on a piece of paper.
After I leave town, you can read it. Then you'll know where to look."
Mary Jane gave me some paper and I scribbled:
"I was behind the door and I saw you crying. I felt very sorry for you. I put it in the coffin."
Then I folded up the paper and gave it to her.
I didn't think it would be safe for me and Jim to travel on the river in daylight.
I wanted to wait until dark to get away.
But Mary Jane was such an honest person that I knew she would not be able to hide her feelings all day.
The expression on her face would tell the king and the duke that she knew the truth.
I asked Mary Jane if she could leave the house until evening.
She agreed to visit her friend Hannah Proctor.
She left quickly before the king and the duke woke up.
At breakfast, I told everyone that Hannah Proctor had the mumps and explained that Mary Jane had gone to look after her.
In the afternoon, I watched the auction in the town square.
By late in the day, almost everything belonging to Peter Wilks had been sold.
But I knew that no money would be paid on the day of the auction.
The duke and the king would have to stay for another day to collect it.
Before that could happen, Mary Jane would come back.
She would tell the truth, and the two scoundrels would be arrested.
By then, I would be safe on the river again with Jim.
I was quite proud of myself and thought I had arranged things very well.
Then I heard loud voices coming toward the center of town.
I turned and saw a well-dressed older gentleman and a nice-looking younger one with his right arm in a sling.
Some townspeople were with them, and one of them called out, "Here are two more men who say they are Harvey Wilks and his brother William!"
Wouldn't you think that the king and the duke would give up when they saw the real Englishmen?
Well, they didn't! The king said in an angry voice, "These men are liars trying to steal our property. Don't listen to them!"
I could see that some townspeople believed the king, but Doctor Robinson and some others looked pleased to see the newcomers.
They had never believed that the duke and the king were honest men.
The two new arrivals were very confused by the uproar.
Harvey Wilks, the older gentleman, told their story:
