They had come all the way from England to see their dying brother, but they had been delayed when poor William broke his arm.
The king demanded to see written proof of who they were.
Harvey replied that this was impossible because their bags had been lost on the journey.
So it went on for a while with both pairs of men claiming they were the true relatives.
I knew the truth, but if I told it, I'd be in trouble too.
Then I wouldn’t be able to get away and help Jim.
Finally, Harvey Wilks said that Peter, his brother, had a small tattoo on his chest.
He challenged the king to describe it. "Why, yes," said the king, "he has a small lightning bolt on his chest."
"No," said the old gentleman. "It is his initials: P and W."
By now, most of the townspeople were so confused that they did not know what to believe.
Doctor Robinson jumped up onto the table that had been used for the auction.
"There's only one way to settle this," he shouted.
"Let's all go to the cemetery and dig up the corpse.
Grab the four men and the boy and make them come with us."
I was very scared, but a townsman was holding me so hard that I couldn't escape.
"If we don't find the tattoo those two scoundrels described, we'll hang you along with them!" he growled at me.
It was dark and windy in the cemetery, and lightning flashed in the sky.
So many men were helping that it did not take long to dig up the grave.
Then they pulled out the coffin and opened the lid.
A huge lightning bolt lit up the night, and someone yelled, "Look at that—there's a big bag of gold on his chest!"
Everyone became so excited that they rushed toward the coffin.
The townsman forgot to hold my wrist, and I ran away at once, down the road as fast as I could.
I ran right through town without seeing anyone.
When I got to the riverbank, a lightning flash showed me a canoe that was pulled up on shore.
I jumped in and paddled until I came to the raft where Jim was waiting.
I had never been so glad to see anyone in my whole life.
"Cut the rope loose and let's go, Jim!" I yelled, climbing aboard.
"We're finally free of those scoundrels."
In seconds, we were out on the river again.
I felt so relieved that I began to jump and dance on the raft.
Then I heard the sound of paddling behind the raft.
The next lightning flash revealed the truth.
It was the duke and the king in a rowboat, catching up with us.
The king and the duke climbed aboard the raft.
The king grabbed my collar and shook me.
"Trying to get away from us, were you?"
"No, Your Majesty, we weren't! Please let me go and I'll tell you the truth," I said.
I quickly made up a story: "The man who was holding me felt sorry for me.
He told me to run away or I would be hanged at once.
I thought you two would be hanged, so Jim and I left.
But we're both very glad to see you alive."
Jim agreed eagerly, and both men seemed to calm down.
They admitted they hadn't thought of trying to save me.
They had run away, too, while everyone was looking at the gold.
"I always thought those slaves that we sold stole the gold," said the king.
"So who do you think put it in the coffin?"
My heart pounded, but the king wasn't looking at me. He was looking angrily at the duke.
"It certainly wasn't me, you old scoundrel!" exclaimed the duke.
"I think it was you, trying to keep the gold for yourself!"
In seconds, they were rolling around on the raft, punching each other.
But when the duke began to choke the king, the old man gasped, "All right, I admit it. I did it. Now let me go!"
The king crawled into the hut on the raft and began to drink whiskey.
The duke soon joined him, and they shared the bottle.
After a little while, they both fell asleep, snoring loudly.
Then I finally told Jim everything that had happened.
We were far south on the Mississippi River now and a long way from home.
The next morning, the king and the duke decided to be friends again.
They wanted to think up a new scam and go back to cheating people.
At different towns along the river, they tried putting on plays and giving talks about the evils of drinking alcohol.
They even tried fortune-telling, but nothing was really successful. Now they were running out of money.
For the next few days, the king and the duke spent a lot of their time in the hut, whispering to each other. Jim and I felt very uneasy.
We were afraid that they were planning something even worse than before, but we didn't know what it was.
When we came to a shabby little place called Pikesville, the king said he would go see if anyone in town had heard of the Royal Nonesuch.
If they hadn't, then he and the duke would stage it again because it always earned them lots of money.
He told us that if he didn't come back before noon, it meant everything was all right.
In that case, the duke and I should join him in Pikesville.
The duke seemed nervous after the king left.
He was cranky with Jim and me and impatient.
When noon came and the king had not returned, the duke and I headed into town.
It took us a long time to find the king.
When we finally discovered him in a dirty little tavern, he was drunk.
The duke was furious. The two men started cursing each other, and I ran out of the tavern and down to the riverbank.
"Jim," I called, "this is our chance to get away from those scoundrels. Untie the rope and let's go!"
But there was no answer. No one came out of the hut on the raft.
I ran up and down the wooded shoreline screaming for Jim.
It was no use; he was gone. I sat down on the bank and cried.
When I realized that crying wouldn't help me, I stopped.
I started down the road away from town, and I met a boy.
I asked him if he had seen a black man, and I described Jim's clothes.
Yes, he said, he'd seen that man. He was a runaway slave.
A man named Silas Phelps had bought him from an old man for forty dollars.
The old man had shown Silas a poster about the slave.
It said the slave had run away from a plantation near New Orleans.
Whoever took him back there would get a two-hundred-dollar reward.
But the old man said he was too tired to go any farther, and that was why he was giving Phelps such a bargain.
I had to sit down and think. I realized that the old man was the king.
I remembered the poster that the duke had printed, describing Jim as a runaway slave.
And now I reckoned that the king had waited for the duke and me to leave the raft, and then came back for Jim and used the poster to sell him.
I felt sick at heart. I was only a boy. What could I do to save Jim?
Maybe I had done all I could. Maybe I should write to Miss Watson and tell her where Jim was.
After all, he was her property. That was the law.
I told myself that if Jim had to be a slave again, he would be happier back home with people he knew. Here, he didn't know anyone.
But then I remembered how Jim had called me his friend.
I thought about how much he wanted to be free and see his family again.
And I decided that I wouldn't write to Miss Watson.
Even if the law said it was wrong, I was going to find a way to help free him.
After a while, I came up with a plan to find Jim. But I had a few things to do first.
I took the raft about a kilometer down the river and hid it in bushes on the shore.
I spent the night there, safe from the duke and the king.
The next morning, I changed into my good clothes—the ones that the two scoundrels had bought me.
I wrapped my other belongings into a bundle and hid it on the riverbank too. Then I set out for Pikesville.
The first person I saw was the duke.
He was hammering up a sign for the Royal Nonesuch.
"I'm very glad to see you," said the duke.
"We couldn't find you and the raft last night."
"Oh," I lied, "I was helping a man move some sheep downriver, and the raft sank. It's gone."
The duke looked unhappy about that, but there was nothing he could do.
"I'm looking for Jim," I continued. "I can't find him anywhere."
"The king, the old fool, sold him for forty dollars," the duke said.
"And by the time you and I reached the tavern yesterday, he had already lost the money by gambling.
That's why we have to put on the Royal Nonesuch again—we have no money."
"But Jim was my property!" I protested. "You must tell me who bought him."
The duke lied. He gave me the wrong name for the owner and gave me the wrong directions to find his house.
He said it would take me three days to reach the home of the man who had bought Jim.
I realized that the duke didn't want me around anymore.
It was time for me to get away for good.
When the duke walked away to put up more signs, I asked someone how to get to Mr. Phelps' house.
It was very near Pikesville, and I arrived quickly.
The house was tidy, with a large fenced yard and a row of little slave cabins behind it.
No one was in sight. It was mid-morning, so the slaves were likely working in the cotton fields already.
As I walked into the yard, a pack of dogs surrounded me, barking loudly.
A black servant ran out of the kitchen, waving a rolling pin, and made the dogs go away.
A moment later, a white lady hurried out of the house, followed by several small children.
She smiled at me and exclaimed, "It's you, at last! We're so happy to finally meet you."
I was surprised, but I decided to play along.
"Me too," I said, as she gave me a big hug.
"Look, children. This is your cousin Tom," she said, and they hugged me too.
"I'm sorry I was delayed, ma'am," I said, thinking quickly.
"The boat I was traveling on got caught on a sandbar.
I had to get off and walk the rest of the way."
"Please, call me Aunt Sally," she said and brought me into the house.
She asked where my baggage was, and I said that I'd left it on the riverbank, where I could get it later.
Aunt Sally explained that her husband, Mr. Silas Phelps, had gone to the boat dock to meet me.
Then she said, "But I've been talking too much.
Please tell me all the news about my sister and the rest of the family."
Now I was in trouble! But before I could say anything, Aunt Sally jumped up from her chair.
"There's Uncle Silas now," she said. "I hear his wagon coming into the yard."
She hurried outside, and I heard her call, "Silas, who do you think has arrived while you were gone? It's our nephew—Tom Sawyer!"
Uncle Silas came inside and shook my hand eagerly.
Then the whole family asked me questions about my Aunt Polly and my brother, Sid.
Now that I knew they thought I was Tom Sawyer, it was easy to answer their questions.
It was very pleasant to be treated so kindly.
But I knew the good times couldn't last. The real Tom would soon arrive.
How could I stop him from giving away my true identity?
I decided I'd have to meet Tom on the road before he reached the house.
I would explain that I wanted to free Jim, and he would help me make a plan.
I asked Uncle Silas if I could take his wagon and go down the road to get my baggage, and he agreed. Off I went.
As I had hoped, I saw Tom coming toward me on the road.
As he got close to the wagon, I called out to him.
Tom dropped his bag and stared at me in horror.
"I never did you any harm," he cried. "Please don't come back and haunt me!"
"It's me—Huck," I said, "and I'm not dead."
I let Tom pinch my arm to see that I was really alive and not a ghost.
He was very surprised to see me, and very happy too.
On the way back to the Phelps' place, I told him all the things that had happened to me since I had run away from Pap.
Then I explained how I had fooled his aunt and uncle, and why I had to keep fooling them until I found a way to rescue Jim.
"I know the law says it's stealing," I said, "but I have to do it. Will you help me?"
Tom Sawyer smiled at me. "Yes, Huck," he said. "Of course I'll help you."
He was quiet for a few minutes thinking.
Then he grinned and told me how I could keep pretending to be Tom Sawyer.
I thought his plan just might work. I never knew anyone better at thinking up plans than Tom.
Soon we were back at the Phelps' house. "Well, who's this?" Aunt Sally asked when we came in the door.
All the little cousins gathered around, looking at us curiously.
"This is my brother, Sid," I said. "I wanted his visit to be a surprise.
That's why I had to go back to the dock—to get him and bring him here."
Aunt Sally looked really surprised. "We're certainly happy to see you," she said, "but my sister's letter said only Tom would be visiting."
"That's right," said the real Tom. "But I begged and begged Aunt Polly to let me come, and at the last minute she finally agreed. So here I am!"
Aunt Sally gave him a big hug. Then she called Uncle Silas to come and meet Sid.
They were nice people, and it never occurred to them that they were being tricked.
The Phelpses fed us a delicious dinner with enough food for seven families.
Tom and I had agreed that we must not ask about Jim because we weren't supposed to know about him.
But we hoped that someone would mention him. Finally, during dinner, someone did.
One of my little cousins asked, "Pa, may Tom and Sid and I go to the show in town?"
"No," said Uncle Silas. "I heard from the runaway slave that it is a stupid show.
He said those two actors have been cheating people all along the river.
I warned a man in town, and he said the townspeople would capture the rascals this evening and throw them out of town."
Now Tom and I knew that Jim really was nearby.
I said that my brother and I were tired, and we went up to our bedroom right after dinner.
"I've got to warn the king and the duke," I told Tom. "They don't know that they're in danger."
We climbed out of our bedroom window and slid down the lightning rod that ran up the side of the house.
We ran down the road, but when we reached the town, we met a noisy, angry crowd.
Some of them were carrying a long pole, with two fellows tied up and hanging underneath it.
They were covered from head to toe with tar and feathers.
It was hard to recognize them, but I knew they must be the king and the duke.
Even though they were scoundrels, I felt sad to see them being treated so roughly.
Tom and I saw that we couldn't do anything to help, so we turned back.
At first we were quiet, thinking about the two men as we walked.
Then Tom said, "I think I know where Jim is!"
"Where?" I asked.
"In that shed behind the kitchen. Didn't you see the servant go out the back door while we were eating?
He was carrying some food. Who do you think it was for?"
"I don't know," I said. "Maybe for the dogs?"
"No, he must be locked in the shed," Tom continued.
"When we were getting up from the table, the servant brought Uncle Silas a big key, and he put it in his pocket."
I couldn't believe how smart Tom was. He had figured out everything.
"So how should we rescue Jim?" Tom asked.
"Let's find out from the servant whether Jim is really in the shed," I said.
"Then, tomorrow night, when Uncle Silas is asleep, we'll take the key from his pocket.
He leaves his trousers hanging on the chair in his bedroom.
We'll free Jim and run down to the riverbank where the raft is hidden.
We'll all get aboard and escape down the river. Wouldn't that work?"
"It might work," said Tom, looking very disappointed. "But it's too simple."
Then Tom told me his plan, which had lots of things to do and would take quite a while.
I thought his plan would probably free Jim, but it might also get us killed.
However, I was so grateful to him for helping me that I didn't object.
When we got back, the house was dark and still, so we tiptoed around to the shed.
On the back wall of the shed, we saw a high square window with a board nailed across it.
"We can pull off that board," I said, "and then Jim can squeeze out the window."
"I hope we can think of an escape that's more interesting than that!" said Tom scornfully.
Next to the shed was a small unlocked hut.
We opened the door, struck a match, and looked inside.
We saw rusty old tools, including spades and picks.
"Now I know what we can do," said Tom happily.
"We can dig Jim out. It will only take about a week."
The back door of the house wasn't locked, so I entered quietly and went up to the bedroom.
But Tom, who always wanted adventures, was determined to climb up the lightning rod and through the window.
After he slipped and fell three times, I finally persuaded him to use the stairs like me.
The next morning, Tom and I got up very early and went down to the kitchen.
We patted the dogs by the back door, and we talked to the black servant who had used the key the night before.
We watched him fixing a tray of food, and we asked if it was for the dogs.
"No," he said with a smile. "Would you like to see who it's for?"
"Yes," said Tom, and we followed the servant out to the shed.
As soon as he unlocked the door, we ran inside. Jim's leg was chained to the bed.
He recognized us right away, but I made a sign for him to be quiet.
I didn't want anyone to guess that we knew him.
The servant put down the tray and left.
We just had a moment to whisper to Jim that we were going to set him free and then we had to leave.
It was still too early for breakfast, so Tom and I went into the woods.
We gathered some chunks of rotting wood with glowing fungus that people call "foxfire."
We could use them to give us a little light while we dug at night.
"A lantern would be too bright," said Tom.
I was happy that our plan was going so well, but Tom was not.
"There ought to be more to do," he said.
"I wish Uncle Silas had put a guard on the shed door because then we could drug him." Then he smiled.
"I know what we can do. We can make a ladder out of torn sheets and take it to Jim hidden inside a big pie.
He can hide the ladder in his mattress until he needs it."
"But he doesn't need a ladder," I said. "We're going to dig him out."
"In a book I read once about escapes, there was a ladder hidden in a pie," retorted Tom.
"We have to do things the right way."
He told me to take a sheet from the clothesline when Aunt Sally wasn't looking.
"And take a shirt too," he said, "for Jim to write a journal on. Prisoners always keep journals."
After breakfast, when no one was in the yard, I borrowed the sheet and the shirt.
Tom and I put them in an old sack along with the foxfire and took the sack into the hut.
"Now all we need is something to dig with," said Tom.
"Look around us," I said. "There are picks and shovels here."
Tom looked at me with contempt. "When heroes are trying to escape in books, they never have shovels."
"Well, if we don't use shovels, what do we use?" I asked.
"Pocketknives," said Tom.
"We're going to dig under that shed with pocketknives?" I asked incredulously.
"That's crazy, Tom!" I was starting to become annoyed with him.
"I read a book once about a man who dug himself out of a castle—it took him 37 years," said Tom.
"We can't take that long," I protested. "Uncle Silas has written to New Orleans to tell the plantation he has their runaway slave.
Soon he'll get a letter explaining that Jim isn't from there."
Tom paused to think and then smiled at me.
"We'll just have to dig faster," he said. It did no good to argue with Tom.
So I borrowed some pocketknives from the house, as he asked me to.
That night, after everyone was asleep, we went to the hut and started digging with the knives.
The hut was right next to Jim's shed. We planned to come up under Jim's bed.
We dug until about midnight. Our hole wasn't very deep, and our hands were blistered.
At last Tom sighed and said, "I hate to do it, but I think we'll have to use the shovels.
We can pretend that we're using the knives."
The next night, using the tools in the hut, we dug all the way through to Jim's shed.
We lit a candle that we had borrowed from the house.
Jim was so relieved to see us that he hugged us and almost cried.
He wanted us to take him out of his prison right away.
I looked at Jim's chain and saw that we could free him if we lifted his bed and slipped the chain off the leg of the bed.
I wanted to do it, but Tom told Jim that we had other things to do first.
Jim told us that he thought it would be all right to wait.
He said that Aunt Sally and Uncle Silas visited him every day to make sure that he was comfortable.
He was getting decent food, enough water, and clean sheets from the servants.
Tom explained that we would be sending Jim a pie with a ladder hidden inside.
He also gave Jim the shirt I had borrowed from the clothesline.
He told Jim that he should write a journal on it with his blood.
"Tom, you're a good boy," said Jim, "but these things make no sense to me."
I tried to explain. "Tom wants us to have an adventure, just like the ones in books.
But trust me, Jim, we know how to free you.
If you are in any danger, we'll get you out right away."
Tom's thirst for adventure was making me nervous.
But I was so grateful to him for helping that I went along with his wild schemes.

episodes.title: A Pie, Some Rats, and Some Snakes

subtitle.text: Early the next morning, Tom and I searched the rubbish heap in the backyard and found an old tin washtub.
We decided that we could use it to bake our big pie in.
We hid it in the hut, and then went into the house.
No one was in the kitchen yet, so we borrowed a spoon.
Tom said Jim could use it to scratch a sad message on his wall.
Later at breakfast, Aunt Sally looked red-faced and cross.
She said to Uncle Silas, "I've looked everywhere for your clean shirt, but I can't find it."
A piece of cornbread stuck in my throat, and I choked a little.
"That's not the only thing that's gone," she said.
"Somehow I've lost one of my best spoons.
Candles are missing from the cellar, too. But rats might have taken those.
Silas, I've asked you many times to plug the holes in the cellar so that they can't come in."
Uncle Silas apologized to his wife and said he would plug the holes that day.
Just then, a young black servant came into the kitchen and told Aunt Sally that a sheet was missing. At that, Aunt Sally grew very angry.
"Out of my kitchen, all of you!" she yelled.
That night, Tom and I put the sheet back on the line.
Then we snuck into the closet and took a different sheet.
We kept doing this for several days—taking a sheet from one place and putting one back in the other.
By the end of three days, Aunt Sally was so confused that she didn't know how many sheets she had.
She stopped complaining about the missing sheet.
We tore up the sheet and braided the strips together to make a rope ladder.
We pretended that it had taken us nine months to make it.
Next we had to bake a pie to hide the ladder in and give it to Jim.
That night, we borrowed flour from the kitchen.
The next day, we took it and the washtub into the woods, and we built a campfire to bake the pie.
The tub was large, but we needed a big pie to hide our ladder.
It was hard work. We didn't put anything inside the pie because we wanted to leave room for the ladder.
But the top crust kept collapsing, and we kept having to start again.
Finally, we realized that we had to bake the pie with the ladder already inside, and that is what we did.
Then we took the huge pie through the hole we'd dug and gave it to Jim.
We told him to be very careful eating the pie, so that he didn't chew the ladder.
And we told him that he should hide the ladder in his mattress. Jim agreed.
Tom said that he thought our plan was going very well.
But Jim hadn't yet used the spoon to scratch a sad message on the wall.
Tom made a list of things Jim might write, and his voice trembled with emotion when he read them to me:
1. Here, a captive heart broke.
2. Here, a poor prisoner, forgotten by the world, lived out his sad life.
3. Here, a lonely soul went to its rest, after 37 years of being a prisoner.
I agreed that they were very sad, but I saw a problem.
He doesn't know how to read or write.
Tom said that he would outline the letters on the wall, and Jim could trace over them.
The next night, we visited Jim again.
Tom told Jim that he really ought to have some spiders, or maybe some rats or snakes, in his prison.
Tom said that prisoners in books always had creatures like this.
"You could make them your pets," Tom said.
Jim thought this was a very bad idea, and so did I.
But I still didn't stop Tom. I wish I had.
The next day, we went down to the cellar and opened one of the holes Uncle Silas had mended.
Tom and I caught 16 rats in a wire cage and hid them under our bed.
However, the latch on our cage door popped open, and they all escaped.
It took us quite a while to catch 16 more.
We caught a few garter snakes too, and some of them got free in the house.
The whole family was becoming very nervous, with rats and snakes popping out when they weren't expecting them.
Meanwhile, we also caught spiders, frogs, and caterpillars.
We put all the creatures in Jim's shed.
Every time a rat gave Jim a little nip, he'd make a mark on the shirt in his blood.
Jim was kept very busy satisfying Tom's need for adventure.
"There's only one thing left to do, now," said Tom.
"We have to send the family a mysterious warning, like they do in books."
So that same night, we pushed a note under the front door to the house.
It read: BEWARE. Trouble is coming. Someone is going to try to steal the escaped slave. From your unknown friend.
The next night, we drew a coffin on the back door. By now the Phelpses were very nervous.
They jumped at every noise, and if anything brushed against them, they thought it was a snake.
They asked some neighbors to help them guard their house.
That evening, there were 15 farmers, armed with guns, sitting in the parlor.
Some of the men said they were going to go down to the shed and guard it.
That's when I knew that Tom had gone too far with his crazy plan.
We should have freed Jim days ago. In a panic, Tom and I ran to the hut.
We went through our tunnel to Jim's shed and told him we had to escape right away.
Suddenly, we heard men outside the door, putting the key in the lock.
Just as they pushed the door open, we hurried into the tunnel.
The men didn't see the hole because it was under Jim's bed.
In the dark, we crept out of the hut and ran across the yard.
Jim and I got over the fence, but Tom's pants caught on a splinter of wood.
The splinter broke off with a loud snap and Tom was free.
But one of the men yelled, "Who's there? Stop, or I'll shoot!"
Bullets whizzed over our heads as we ran through the woods.
We hid behind some bushes until the men gave up looking for us.
Then we scrambled down the riverbank, untied the raft, and got onboard.
We headed for the middle of the river, to a small island called Spanish Island.
"Well, Jim," I said, "you are a free man.
I hope you won't ever be a slave again."
We were both happy for a minute, until we saw that Tom had been shot in the leg!
Jim and I helped him into the hut on the raft.
We bandaged Tom's bleeding calf with one of the duke's old shirts.
Then we looked at each other with serious faces.
Jim said, "Huck, we have to get a doctor for Tom.
Even if it means that I am captured again."
I knew Jim was right. I paddled back to the shore in the canoe that we kept on the raft. Jim and Tom stayed behind.
The town doctor was a kind man. Even though I woke him up late at night, he dressed and came with me right away.
I made up a story that my brother Sid and I had been hunting on the island.
There had been an accident with Sid's gun, I said.
When the doctor saw the old canoe, however, he didn't think it was safe for two people.
He said that he would paddle over to the raft by himself.
I waited for a long time, but the doctor didn't come back. I was worried about Tom's wound.
Then I realized that it was morning; I had fallen asleep on the riverbank.
I went to the doctor's house and learned that he still hadn't come back.
I decided that I had to find out how Tom was, even if I had to swim to the island.
But as I was hurrying down the street, I met Uncle Silas.
"Why, Tom!" he exclaimed. "Your aunt and I have been so worried about you and Sid. Where have you been all night?"
Once again, I made up a story. I told Uncle Silas that Sid and I had run to help the men chase the runaway slave.
But we lost them in the dark woods.
We were so tired that we fell asleep there.
I said that Sid had gone to buy rolls for our breakfast from the bakery.
As soon as Sid came back, we were planning to go home to Aunt Sally.
Uncle Silas said we must go to the bakery to get Sid. But of course he wasn't there.
Finally, Uncle Silas said that we shouldn't wait any longer to get me home, where Aunt Sally was waiting anxiously.
Then he would go out to search for Sid.
Aunt Sally was so happy to see me that she cried and hugged me.
She was very upset that Sid wasn't with us, but I told the same story again. Uncle Silas went out again to search.
The hours went by. Aunt Sally was worried because her nephew was lost.
I knew he wasn't lost, but I was afraid he was dying.
I couldn't tell anyone, though, because if they found Tom, they would find Jim and make him a slave again.
By dinnertime, Uncle Silas hadn't returned. By bedtime, he still wasn't back. I went up to my room and cried.
Later Aunt Sally stopped by my room.
"I know how worried you are," she said, "but I want you to promise that you won't sneak out to look for Sid."
She was a good, kind person, so I promised.
When I came down to breakfast, Uncle Silas and Aunt Sally were sitting at the table, looking sad.
Then, we all heard noises in the yard and ran outside.
It was Tom! The doctor and some other men were carrying him on a mattress.
Jim was there, too, with his hands tied behind his back.
He was surrounded by the men who had chased us two nights ago.
Aunt Sally became very busy, giving orders to servants and getting a bed ready for Tom.
Meanwhile, the men were treating Jim roughly.
One of them even said he should be hanged because of the trouble he had caused.
But another man said, no, the slave didn't belong to them, and his owner would be very angry if he didn't get his property back.
Jim pretended that he didn't know me. I felt terribly sad that I couldn't help him.
I was very relieved when the doctor told the men to treat him kindly.
"He's a good man," the doctor said. "He could have run away, but he stayed with me the whole time.
He was a good nurse to that boy and helped me save his life."
After that the men were kinder to Jim, but they still put chains on him and locked him in the shed again.
The doctor told me that Tom was going to be fine.
But I knew I still had a lot to worry about.
How would I explain why I didn't tell the Phelpses that Sid was shot? How could I help to free Jim?
The next day, Tom was so much better that I was allowed to go see him in his room.
He was sitting up in bed, and he began to talk to me and Aunt Sally.
He was not very alert after his gunshot wound and his fever.
I quickly realized he had forgotten that we were keeping many things secret.
"How's Jim?" he said to me.
"He's fine," I said quietly, frowning at him to show that he should be quiet. But he kept on talking.
"Have you told Aunt Sally how we did everything?" continued Tom.
"Did what?" asked Aunt Sally, looking suspicious.
Then, Tom told the whole story: the escape plan, the things we borrowed, the tunnel we had dug.
Aunt Sally was astonished. When she realized how much trouble we had caused, she started to look angry.
But Tom kept smiling. ". . . and so we helped the runaway slave get away," he finished.
"But he didn't get away," said Aunt Sally.
"He's locked in the shed right now."
Tom's face grew red. "No, that's not right! You have to let him go.
Old Mrs. Watson died two months ago, and in her will, she set Jim free.
He's a free man, as free as you and me!"
Aunt Sally opened her mouth to speak, when someone else hurried into the room.
"Why, sister!" she exclaimed. I turned to look, and there was Tom's Aunt Polly!
While the two sisters were hugging, I hid under the bed.
"Come out from there, Huck Finn!" commanded Aunt Polly.
"What mischief have you and Tom been making now?"
Aunt Sally was very confused. "But that's Tom under the bed, and Sid in the bed!"
"I certainly know my own nephew Tom—I've looked after him since he was a baby," said Aunt Polly.
"And I know Huckleberry, too! When I got that letter from you saying Sid was visiting, I had to come and see what was wrong.
Sid is safe at home, where he should be."
The first chance I got to talk to Tom by himself, I asked him why he never told us that Jim was a free man.
"I wanted to have adventures," Tom said. "I wanted to free him from prison.
Then, I wanted to go down the Mississippi on the raft with you and him.
I planned to wait until we got to New Orleans and then tell Jim the truth."
Aunt Sally and Uncle Silas freed Jim from the shed as soon as they heard Tom's story.
They fed him a good meal and gave him some clean clothes.
Then Tom gave Jim forty dollars to start his new life.
"Remember what I told you, Huck?" Jim said to me.
"If a man has hair on his chest like me, it means he is going to be rich some day. And now I am!"
Once Tom was feeling better, he wanted Jim to stay for a few days.
"We could dress up and pretend to be pirates," Tom suggested.
"I don't have any money for pirate clothes.
I guess by now Pap got all our money from Judge Thatcher," I said.
"No, he hasn't," said Tom. "We still have our six thousand dollars.
Pap hasn't come back—at least, he hadn't when I left home."
Then, Jim said in a serious voice, "Your Pap isn't ever coming back, Huck. You don't have to worry about that."
At first, he didn't want to explain how he knew this, but I wouldn't stop asking questions.
Finally Jim said, "Do you remember that house that we found, floating down the river?"
I nodded.
"Do you remember that there was a body inside, and I told you not to look?
Well, I recognized his face—it was your Pap."
Well, now I've finished everything I wanted to write.
Tom's leg has healed. And he kept the bullet for a souvenir.
Aunt Sally wants to adopt me and civilize me. But I might run away.
I've already been civilized once, and I don't think I like it.
